timing_rule: Latest eligible year per source within 3 years; dated fieldwork must end before the decision, otherwise an earlier calendar year is required. Retain all eligible question variants in that year.

contribution_priority.support_definition: Original policy categories retained; contextual only, no alignment score.

disclosure.support_definition: Original policy categories retained; contextual only, no alignment score.

aggregate_candidate_limits.support_definition: Two questions from one sample: preference about a stated total candidate cap and whether total candidate limits violate free speech. Retain separately; no ruling-approval score.

cases.name: Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission

components.decision: The Court invalidated restrictions on independent corporate and union election spending.
components.scope: Independent expenditures differ from donations directly to candidates; the ruling did not legalize unrestricted direct corporate donations.
components.survey_fit: The survey contrasts contribution limits with freedom to support campaigns. It does not isolate independent expenditures; no agreement rate with the holding can be calculated.

observations.wording: Prioritizing contribution limits or the freedom of individuals, corporations and unions to support campaigns.
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased question. Gallup/First Amendment Center. Chart prints 52% and 41% only. The 7% remainder is calculated as 100−52−41; its response category is not reported, so it is not labeled unsure. Survey total was 1,023, with split forms; the item base is not identified here. Published after Citizens United, but fielded before it.
observations.denominator: National adult telephone sample; original response shares retained.
observations.orientation: Policy context only; not approval of the specific holding.

components.decision: The Court upheld the challenged disclosure and disclaimer requirements.
components.scope: This separate part of the decision prevents treating the entire judgment as eliminating campaign-finance regulation.
components.survey_fit: No earlier question about these disclosure requirements is included; leave this component unscored.

cases.name: McCutcheon v. Federal Election Commission

components.decision: The Court struck down the total a donor could contribute across candidates and committees.
components.scope: Per-recipient base limits were not struck down. Four justices joined Roberts’s reasoning; Thomas supplied the fifth vote with a separate rationale.
components.locator: Roberts opinion, Parts II–IV; Thomas concurrence.
components.survey_fit: The earlier poll explicitly measures total donations across candidates, a closer match than candidate fundraising. It quotes a $46,200 cap, not the updated $48,600 candidate cap, and omits party/committee totals. The speech question addresses candidate totals, not every part of the holding. Both questions share one sample; retain contextual fit and do not calculate ruling approval.

observations.weight: Published topline from a demographically matched opt-in online panel; no respondent-level recalculation.
observations.denominator: All 1,000 U.S. adult interviews, including not sure. Published percentages retained; the two questions share the same sample.
observations.wording: Whether a $46,200 total cap on donations to federal candidates is too high, too low, appropriate, or should not exist.
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased summary. The prompt explicitly applies across candidates regardless of how many are supported. It quotes $46,200, not the updated $48,600 candidate cap or the $123,200 combined candidate/committee cap discussed in the ruling. It does not expressly state a time period. Q1 first asks about a $2,600 per-candidate limit. Field dates, sample and online-panel method are corroborated by the February 22, 2013 HuffPost report.
observations.orientation: Preferences about an aggregate candidate cap; too low still permits a cap and must not be combined with no limit.

observations.weight: Published topline from a demographically matched opt-in online panel; no respondent-level recalculation.
observations.denominator: All 1,000 U.S. adult interviews, including not sure. Published percentages retained; the two questions share the same sample.
observations.wording: Whether limits on an individual’s total donations to candidates violate free-speech rights.
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased summary. Asked after per-candidate and aggregate-limit questions and a question about preventing corruption. Wording covers candidate totals, not party and PAC totals or the Court’s full reasoning. It measures an opinion about rights, not respondent legal expertise. Field dates, sample and online-panel method are corroborated by the February 22, 2013 HuffPost report.
observations.orientation: Yes regards total candidate limits as a speech violation; no does not. Neither is approval or disapproval of the later ruling.

response_distribution.label: No — does not violate free speech

cases.interpretation_limit: The two-year aggregate limits were invalidated; per-recipient base limits remained. The two poll items are not independent corroboration. Their sequence and the quoted dollar amount matter.

limitations: Explicit source-based legal coding is an input, not an automated legal classifier.
Contextual matches do not measure approval of the specific holding.
Mixed and unresolved components retain their labels; no scalar direction is inferred.
No pooling, confidence intervals, causal claims, or prediction.
